Rising in the densely forested interior, the river flows towards the Atlantic coast, shaping natural environments closely connected with the lives of local communities.

The river plays an important part in the region's economy. Its waters and banks form part of local transport routes, while the surrounding land is used for agriculture. Farther from populated areas, the scenery grows greener and more secluded, revealing the distinctive natural environment of Suriname's tropics.

The banks of the Saramacca are lined with varied vegetation, and the river itself supports many species of local wildlife. Here you can experience a distinctive pace of life in Suriname, where natural conditions strongly shape people's daily routines.

Travelling along the river reveals another side of South America, far from crowded resorts and bustling cities, among open stretches of water, dense forest and small settlements.

The Saramacca River offers a chance to discover Suriname's natural wealth and get to know the distinctive world of its tropical river valleys.

The Rupununi Savannahs cover almost the entire southwestern part of Guyana, stretching from the ancient equatorial forests of the Guiana Plateau to the tropical jungles of the Amazon.

## Tour of the Rupununi Savannahs

### Guyana's rich natural world!

The Rupununi Savannahs boast remarkable biodiversity. Around 250 species of birds live here, 18 of them endemic, alongside jaguars and harpy eagles. These strikingly beautiful savannahs, interspersed with forested hills, crossed by numerous freshwater streams and dotted with termite mounds and riverside groves, are regarded as the continent's largest expanse of ancient grasslands.

Schollaert Channel lies between Anvers Island to the southwest and Brabant Island to the northeast. One of the waterways of the Palmer Archipelago, it connects Dallmann Bay with the Gerlache Strait. The passage offers views of glaciated island shores, rocky ridges and floating ice.

The channel was discovered in 1898 by the Belgian Antarctic Expedition led by Adrien de Gerlache. It was named after Frans Schollaert, who served as Belgium's minister of the interior when the expedition set out. For travellers, this is first and foremost part of a sea route; the time taken to cross it and opportunities for viewing from the deck depend on the weather and ice conditions.

## Ciego de Ávila — a Cuban beach resort

The city and the province of the same name, Ciego de Ávila, lie in the centre of the island. Numerous reefs and islands line the province's northern coast, where beach resorts have been established to welcome visitors.

## Things to do in Ciego de Ávila

Ciego de Ávila province is known as a 'pineapple paradise' because the fruit grows here in abundance. There are plenty of opportunities for active holidays, including horseback excursions, boat trips, diving and sport fishing. The city contains many buildings with arches and columns, giving its architecture a distinctive look. Landmarks include the Principal Theatre, the Raúl Martínez Art Gallery and the cathedral. Arts-and-crafts fairs and markets selling traditional handmade goods are also very popular.
